# Iteration

In this week's lesson, we will be talking about how to do repetitive tasks.

As it turns out, computers are really good at repeating tasks. We call this repetition of the same task "iteration."

There are many ways to iterate in R (we will look at a few others at the end of the lesson), but this week focuses on loops, which give us complete control over any kind of repetition we want. Specifically, we will use `for` loops, which perform the same action for each item in a list of things.

## The `for` Loop

The general structure of a `for` loop is below:

```{r}
# for (item in list_of_items) {
#   do_something(item)
# }
```

To see an example of this, let's calculate biomasses from volumes using a loop. If we want to see the results of the loop, we need to print them out.

```{r}
# vector of volumes
volumes <- c(1.6, 3, 8)

# for each volume value in a vector of volumes
for (vol in volumes){           # perform some task inside the {}
  biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9   # calculate a mass
  print(biomass)                # print out the mass
}
```

The code inside the curly brackets runs once for each value in `volumes`. The `vol` object is a placeholder, representing one value from `volumes` at a time.

The loop takes the first value from `volumes`, assigns it to `vol`, and runs everything inside the curly brackets from top to bottom. Then it starts over with the second value, and so on, until it has run through every element.

Ultimately, the loop above is doing the exact same thing as the code below, but in a more condensed and more flexible way.

```{r}
# same as the for loop above
vol <- volumes[1]
biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
print(biomass)

vol <- volumes[2]
biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
print(biomass)

vol <- volumes[3]
biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
print(biomass)
```

### Let's Practice!

| Work on Questions 1a and 1b in the Assignment.

## Looping with an Index and Storing Results

The loop above uses each value directly; this is called *looping by value*.

There is another way to loop: *looping by index*. Remember sub-setting by index (position) from the beginning of the course? Looping by index loops through position numbers (1, 2, 3...) and uses them to pull values out of a vector with square brackets.

-   We often use `i` (for "index") as the placeholder.
-   We use `1:length(volumes)` so the loop works no matter how many values there are. (For a data frame, we use `nrow()`.)

```{r}
for (i in 1:length(volumes)){       # i takes the values 1, 2, 3
  biomass <- 2.65 * volumes[i] ^ 0.9  # volumes[i] is the ith volume
  print(biomass)
}
```

Same result, but more complicated to read. So why loop by index? The most common reason is to **store the results** in the same order (position) as the values we used to calculate them.

To store results, we create an empty object *before* the loop starts. The `vector()` function makes an empty vector:

-   `mode` is the type of data we are going to store
-   `length` is the number of items in the vector

```{r}
biomasses <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = length(volumes))
biomasses
```

Then, each trip through the loop, we put the output into the `i`th position of the empty vector.

```{r}
for (i in 1:length(volumes)){
   biomass <- 2.65 * volumes[i] ^ 0.9
   biomasses[i] <- biomass
}

biomasses
```

Looping by index also lets us pull values from several vectors at the same position.

```{r}
a_values <- c(2.65, 1.28, 3.29)
b_values <- c(0.9, 1.1, 1.2)

for (i in 1:length(volumes)){
   biomasses[i] <- a_values[i] * volumes[i] ^ b_values[i]
}

biomasses
```

### Let's Practice!

| Work on Questions 1c, 1d, and 1e in the Assignment.

## Looping over Data Frames

Several vectors of the same length, lined up by position...that is exactly what the columns of a data frame are! Most of the time, the values you want to loop over will be in a data frame.

```{r}
data <- data.frame(a = a_values, b = b_values, volume = volumes)
data
```

To loop over rows, we loop by index from 1 to `nrow()`, and use `$` plus `[i]` to grab the value in a specific column for that row. To store results, we can create a new, empty column first.

This is also where loops really shine: we can put an `if`-`else` statement inside a loop. Let's only calculate biomass if the volume is less than 5.

```{r}
data$biomass <- NA   # new, empty column

for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
  if (data$volume[i] < 5) {
    biomass <- data$a[i] * data$volume[i] ^ data$b[i]
  } else {
    biomass <- NA
  }
  data$biomass[i] <- biomass
}

data
```

We can also call a function inside a loop. Remember that functions containing `if`-`else` statements are not vectorized, so we can't just give them a whole column; a loop solves that.

```{r}
est_biomass <- function(volume, a, b){
  if (volume < 5) {
    biomass <- a * volume ^ b
  } else {
    biomass <- NA
  }
  return(biomass)
}

for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
  data$biomass[i] <- est_biomass(data$volume[i], data$a[i], data$b[i])
}

data
```

> **Do you need a loop?** For a calculation within a single data frame, the tidyverse way is usually simpler. `if_else()` is vectorized, so it works inside `mutate()` with no loop:
>
> ```{r}
> data |>
>   dplyr::mutate(biomass = dplyr::if_else(volume < 5, a * volume ^ b, NA))
> ```
>
> Loops are most useful when the repetition goes *beyond* one data frame, like working through many files (coming up next!). We'll see more alternatives to loops at the end of the lesson.

### Let's Practice!

| Work on Question 2 in the Assignment.

## Troubleshooting Loops

Occasionally (okay, maybe often...) when you write a for loop, it will either give you an error or run successfully but give results you didn't anticipate.

Since loops have a placeholder in them (such as `i`), the best way to figure out what is going on is to set the placeholder equal to a specific value and run each line of code between the `{}` one at a time.

What is wrong with the loop below?

```{r}
data$biomass <- NA

for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
  if (data$volume[i] < 5) {
    data$biomass[i] <- data$a[i] * data$volume[i] ^ data$b[i]
  } else {
    data$biomass <- NA
  }
}

data

# in the console, set i to a number; run the code inside the loop line by line
# i <- 2
# i <- 3
```

If part of your loop is working but another part isn't, find a value (or row) that should trigger the part that isn't working and set the index to that.

## Looping over Files

Loops are especially handy when we have many similar files and want to do the same tasks to each one.

To demonstrate, let's download some simulated satellite collar data. Make sure you change the file paths to match the sub-directories in your RStudio Project, as needed.

```{r}
download.file(url = "http://www.datacarpentry.org/semester-biology/data/locations.zip",
              destfile = "../data_raw/locations.zip") # where to put the zip file

# zipfile argument is the location of the file to be unzipped
# exdir argument is the location where the "extracted" files should be placed
unzip(zipfile = "../data_raw/locations.zip", exdir = "../data_raw/")
```

Before we can loop through these files, we need their names. The `list.files()` function lists the files in a directory. The optional `pattern` argument lets us keep only the files we want (and can take regular expressions).

```{r}
# in regex, .* means any character (.) any number of times (*)
# "locations.*.txt" indicates any file starting with "locations" and ending with ".txt"
data_files <- list.files(path = "../data_raw/", pattern = "locations.*.txt")
data_files
```

Let's say we want the file name, the number of observations, and the minimum latitude for each file. Since we are collecting several pieces of information, we'll store them in a data frame.

We start by creating an empty data frame with `data.frame()`. Each argument is one column: `column_name` = an empty vector of the correct type and length.

```{r}
num_files <- length(data_files)

results <- data.frame(file_name = vector(mode = "character", length = num_files),
                      count = vector(mode = "integer", length = num_files),
                      min_lat = vector(mode = "numeric", length = num_files))
results
```

Then we loop over the files, read each one in, and store the information in the `i`th row of the appropriate column.

```{r}
for (i in 1:num_files){

  # read in the data file
  filename <- data_files[i]
  locations <- read.csv(paste0("../data_raw/", filename))

  # add information about the data file into the data frame
  results$file_name[i] <- filename
  results$count[i] <- nrow(locations)
  results$min_lat[i] <- min(locations$lat)

}

results
```

---
title: "Week 13: Iteration"
author: "Ellen Bledsoe"
format: pdf
editor: visual
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

# Iteration

In this week's lesson, we will be talking about how to do repetitive tasks.

As it turns out, computers are really good at repeating tasks. We call this repetition of the same task "iteration."

While our lesson today will focus mainly on one way to iterate in R (`for` loops), there are actually many ways to do so. We'll take a quick look at some of the others at the end of the lesson.

## The `for` Loop

Loops are the fundamental structure for repetition in programming.

In particular, `for` loops perform the same action for each item in a list of things.

The general structure of a `for` loop is below:

```{r}
# for (item in list_of_items) {
#   do_something(item)
# }
```

To see an example of this, let's calculate biomasses from volumes using a loop. If we want to see the results of the loop, we need to print them out. In this loop, we are going to use a `print()` function to display our results for each mass.

```{r}
# vector of volumes
volumes <- c(1.6, 3, 8)

# for each volume value in a vector of volumes
for (vol in volumes){           # perform some task inside the {}
  biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9   # calculate a mass
  print(biomass)                # print out the mass
}
```

The code that is inside of the curly brackets will run once for each value in `volumes`. The `vol` object is a placeholder, representing one value from `volumes` at a time.

Everything between the curly brackets is executed each time through the loop, from top to bottom.

The loop takes the first value from `volumes` and assigns it to the object `vol`. It performs the code inside the curly brackets, calculating the biomass and then printing the result.

Once the code hits the end of what is enclosed inside the curly brackets, it starts the code all over again from the beginning using the next item in the list (or the `volumes` vector, in this case). The code takes the second value from `volumes`, assigns it to `vol`, does the calculation and prints the output.

It continues to repeat this process--running the code with one value, then starting the whole process over again with the next value--until it has run through every element in the list.

Ultimately, the loop above is doing the exact same thing as the code below, but in a more condensed and more flexible way.

```{r}
# same as the for loop above
vol <- volumes[1]
biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
print(biomass)

vol <- volumes[2]
biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
print(biomass)

vol <- volumes[3]
biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
print(biomass)
```

### Let's Practice!

| Work on Questions 1a and 1b in the Assignment.

## Looping with an Index

Loops are iterating over a series of elements in a vector or other list-like object. When we use that value directly, this is called looping by value.

There is another way to loop: *looping by index*

You might remember way back at the beginning of the course that we talked about two different ways to subset data: by index or by condition. Sub-setting based on index meant sub-setting *based on the position* of the item(s) we are interested in.

Looping by index does something similar. It loops through a list of integer index values, typically starting at 1. These integers are then used to access values in one or more vectors *based on the position* indicated by the index.

Let's take our previous loop and modify it to use an index.

-   We often use `i` to stand for "index" as the variable we update with each step through the loop.
-   We don't have to know the length of the vector. We can add flexibility by using a function to count the number of elements that we will want to loop over. For a vector, the `length()` function is useful for this. For a data frame, the `nrow()` function is often used.
-   Then, inside the loop, instead of doing the calculation on the index value (which is a number between 1 and 3 in our case), we use square brackets and the index as a placeholder.

```{r}
volumes <- c(1.6, 3, 8)

for (i in 1:length(volumes)){        # i will be 1, then 2, then 3
   biomass <- 2.65 * volumes[i] ^ 0.9  # volumes[i] is the ith volume
   print(biomass)
}
```

This new version of the loop gives us the same result as our original loop, but it's more complicated to understand. So why would we want to loop by index?

The advantage to looping by index is that it lets us do more complicated things, as we will see below.

### Storing Results

One of the most common reasons we use `for` loops with indices is to store the outputs from the loop. We typically want the results to be in the same order (position) as what we used to calculate them.

To store results, we start by creating an empty object (vector, column, data frame, etc.) before the loop starts. This object should be the same length as the results will be, which is typically the same as the object we are looping over.

To store results in a vector, we can use the function `vector` to create an empty vector of the correct length. For the `vector` function:

-   `mode` is the type of data we are going to store
-   `length` is the number of items in the vector

```{r}
biomasses <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = length(volumes))
biomasses
```

Now that we have a place to store the results, we need to tell the loop to place the results in the correct position in the empty vector. We can use the index to do this.

For each trip through the loop, we want to put the output into the empty vector at the `i`th position.

```{r}
for (i in 1:length(volumes)){

}

Once the code hits the end of what is enclosed inside the curly brackets, it starts the code all over again from the beginning using the next item in the list (or the `volumes` vector, in this case). The loop takes the first value from `volumes` and assigns it to the object `vol`. It performs the code inside the curly brackets, calculating the biomass and then printing the result.

Once the code hits the end of what is enclosed inside the curly brackets, it starts the code all over again from the beginning using the next item in the list (or the `volumes` vector, in this case). The code takes the second value from `volumes`, assigns it to `vol`, does the calculation and prints the output.

It continues to repeat this process--running the code with one value, then starting the whole process over again with the next value--until it has run through every element in the list.

Ultimately, the loop above is doing the exact same thing as the code below, but in a more condensed and more flexible way.

```{r}
# same as the for loop above
vol <- volumes[1]
biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
print(biomass)

vol <- volumes[2]
biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
print(biomass)

vol <- volumes[3]
biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
print(biomass)
```

## Looping with an Index

Loops are iterating over a series of elements in a vector or other list-like object. When we use that value directly, this is called looping by value.

There is another way to loop: *looping by index*

You might remember way back at the beginning of the course that we talked about two different ways to subset data: by index or by condition. Sub-setting based on index meant sub-setting *based on the position* of the item(s) we are interested in.

Looping by index does something similar. It loops through a list of integer index values, typically starting at 1. These integers are then used to access values in one or more vectors *based on the position* indicated by the index.

Let's take our previous loop and modify it to use an index.

-   We often use `i` to stand for "index" as the variable we update with each step through the loop.
-   We don't have to know the length of the vector. We can add flexibility by using a function to count the number of elements that we will want to loop over. For a vector, the `length()` function is useful for this. For a data frame, the `nrow()` function is often used.
-   Then, inside the loop, instead of doing the calculation on the index value (which is a number between 1 and 3 in our case), we use square brackets and the index as a placeholder.

```{r}
volumes <- c(1.6, 3, 8)

for (i in 1:length(volumes)){        # i will be 1, then 2, then 3
   biomass <- 2.65 * volumes[i] ^ 0.9  # volumes[i] is the ith volume
   print(biomass)
}
```

This new version of the loop gives us the same result as our original loop, but it's more complicated to understand. So why would we want to loop by index?

The advantage to looping by index is that it lets us do more complicated things, as we will see below.

### Storing Results

One of the most common reasons we use `for` loops with indices is to store the outputs from the loop. We typically want the results to be in the same order (position) as what we used to calculate them.

To store results, we start by creating an empty object (vector, column, data frame, etc.) before the loop starts. This object should be the same length as the results will be, which is typically the same as the object we are looping over.

To store results in a vector, we can use the function `vector` to create an empty vector of the correct length. For the `vector` function:

-   `mode` is the type of data we are going to store
-   `length` is the number of items in the vector

```{r}
biomasses <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = length(volumes))
biomasses
```

Now that we have a place to store the results, we need to tell the loop to place the results in the correct position in the empty vector. We can use the index to do this.

For each trip through the loop, we want to put the output into the empty vector at the `i`th position.

```{r}
for (i in 1:length(volumes)){
   biomass <- 2.65 * volumes[i] ^ 0.9
   biomasses[i] <- biomass
}

biomasses
```

### Looping over Multiple Values

So far, we've talked about looping through one group of values (in a vector). Looping with an index also allows us to access values from multiple vectors.

```{r}
# vectors
a_values <- c(2.65, 1.28, 3.29)
b_values <- c(0.9, 1.1, 1.2)
volumes <- c(1.6, 3, 8)

# empty vector for results
biomasses <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = length(volumes))

# for loop
for (i in 1:length(volumes)){
   biomass <- a_values[i] * volumes[i] ^ b_values[i]
   biomasses[i] <- biomass
}

biomasses
```

## Looping over Data Frames

Multiple vectors of the same length, lined up by position, are exactly what the columns of a data frame are. Most of the time, the values we want to loop over will be in a data frame.

```{r}
data <- data.frame(a = a_values, b = b_values, volume = volumes)
data
```

To loop over rows, we need to do some extra work. We can loop by index, and if we want to use a specific column, we need to specify the column via sub-setting, as well.

We can create a new, empty column in the data frame. We can also place an `if`-`else` statement directly into the for loop and reference specific columns with the `$` operator and subset by index, as we did above.

```{r}
data$biomass <- NA

for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
  if (data$volume[i] < 5) {
    biomass <- data$a[i] * data$volume[i] ^ data$b[i]
  } else {
    biomass <- NA
  }
  data$biomass[i] <- biomass
}

data
```

Realistically, I find myself putting `if`-`else` statements inside `for` loops, like the structure above, rather frequently.

### Looping with Functions

Another common thing to do is combine loops with functions by calling one or more functions as a step in our loop.

For example, let's take the non-vectorized version of our `est_biomass` function that returns an estimated biomass if the `volume < 5` and `NA` if it is not.

```{r}
est_biomass <- function(volume, a, b){
  if (volume < 5) {
    biomass <- a * volume ^ b
  } else {
    biomass <- NA
  }
  return(biomass)
}
```

We can't pass the vector to the function and get back a vector of results because `if` statements are not vectorized.

Instead, we can loop over the values.

```{r}
for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
  data$biomass[i] <- est_biomass(data$volume[i], data$a[i], data$b[i])
}

data
```

> Do you need a loop? For a calculation within a single data frame, `mutate()` is usually simpler. `if_else()` is vectorized, so it works inside `mutate()` without a loop:
>
> ```{r}
> data |>
>   dplyr::mutate(biomass = dplyr::if_else(volume < 5, a * volume ^ b, NA))
> ```
>
> Loops are most useful when the repetition goes beyond one data frame, like working through many files (coming up below!).

## Troubleshooting Loops

Occasionally (okay, maybe often...) when you write a for loop, it will either give you an error or it will successfully run but the results won't be what you anticipated.

Since loops (like functions) have some kind of placeholder in them (such as `i` for index), what is the best way to figure out what the error is?

I often set my placeholder equal to a specific value and run through each line of code between the `{}` to check every step individually.

```{r}
data$biomass <- NA

for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
  if (data$volume[i] < 5) {
    data$biomass[i] <- data$a[i] * data$volume[i] ^ data$b[i]
  } else {
    data$biomass <- NA
  }
}

data

# in the console, set i = to a number; run the entire code chunk line by line
# i = 2
# i = 3
```

If part of your loop seems to be behaving the way you expect but another part isn't, I often find a value (or row) that should cause the loop to perform the task that isn't working the way you expect and set the index to that value.

## Looping over Files

While we often want to repeat things within our data, either in vectors or data frames, there are other instances when we might want to repeat the same task.

For example, if we have many similar files, we might want to repeat the same tasks for all of those files.

To demonstrate, let's download some simulated satellite collar data. Make sure you change the file paths accordingly to match the sub-directories in your RStudio Project, as needed.

```{r}
download.file(url = "http://www.datacarpentry.org/semester-biology/data/locations.zip",
              destfile = "../data_raw/locations.zip") # where to put the zip file

# unzip() function to open the zip file
# zipfile argument is the location of the file to be unzipped
# exdir argument is the location where the "extracted" files should be placed
unzip(zipfile = "../data_raw/locations.zip", exdir = "../data_raw/")
```

Before we can loop through these files, we need to get the names of all of these files.

We can do so by using the `list.files()` function. We just want the data files we downloaded, so we'll add the optional `pattern` argument to only get the text files (end with `.txt`).

The pattern argument can also take regular expressions if you need to be more nuanced about which files to include.

```{r}
# in regex, .* means any character (.) any number of times (*)
# "locations.*.txt" indicates any file starting with "locations" and ending with ".txt"
data_files <- list.files(path = "../data_raw/", pattern = "locations.*.txt")
data_files
```

### Storing Loop Results in a Data Frame

Often, we want to calculate multiple pieces of information in a loop. When we do this, it is particularly useful to store these results in something other than individual vectors. Instead, we might want to store them in a data frame.

For example, let's say we want to know the file name, count the number of observations, and get the minimum latitude value for each file.

We would start by creating an empty data frame that we will then populate with the results of our loop. We can use the `data.frame` function. Each argument is for one column.

-   `column_name` = an empty vector of the correct type and length

```{r}
num_files <- length(data_files)

results <- data.frame(file_name = vector(mode = "character", length = num_files),
                      count = vector(mode = "integer", length = num_files),
                      min_lat = vector(mode = "numeric", length = num_files))
results
```

Now we can write our loop. To store each value, we first specify which column in the `results` data frame the value should go in using the `$` operator, then the `i`th row (e.g., `results$count[i]`).

```{r}
for (i in 1:num_files){

  # read in the data file
  filename <- data_files[i]
  locations <- read.csv(paste0("../data_raw/", filename))

  # add information about the data file into the data frame
  results$file_name[i] <- filename
  results$count[i] <- nrow(locations)
  results$min_lat[i] <- min(locations$lat)

}

results
```

## Other Ways to Iterate in R

While this lesson focused on `for` loops, there are actually many ways to iterate in R. I've included a quick overview below.

#### 1. Writing Vectorized Functions

We can write functions that take either a single value or a vector of values, do element-wise calculations, and return a vector of results.

Many functions automatically work with either a single value or a vector of values. Each function we wrote in our functions lesson in Week 11 can work with vectors.

NOTE! An important exception is when we use `if`-`else` statements inside our functions; these do not work with vectors.

If you are interested in learning more about vectorized functions, [here](https://towardsdatascience.com/make-your-r-code-10x-faster-vectorization-explained-in-3-minutes-9eb4cdd7a49e/) is a good place to start.

#### 2. Using `apply` or `map` Functions

Both of these are families of functions. They take a function and apply that function to each item in a list of items.

The `apply` functions (e.g., `apply`, `lapply`, `sapply`) are base R; you can learn more about how to use them [here](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2022/03/complete-tutorial-on-using-apply-functions-in-r/).

The `map` functions come from the `purrr` package, part of the `tidyverse`. [Chapter 26: Iteration](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/iteration) in the "R for Data Science (2e)" book is a good starting point, as is the [`purrr` cheatsheet](https://purrr.tidyverse.org/).

```{r}
hot_or_cold <- function(temp){
  if (temp > 72) {
    category <- "hot"
  } else {
    category <- "cold"
  }
  return(category)
}

temps <- c(47.2, 72, 100)

# base R
sapply(temps, hot_or_cold)

# purrr from tidyverse
purrr::map(temps, hot_or_cold)
```

#### 3. In data frames, using `dplyr` (mostly)

We've actually already been iterating quite a bit--specifically in data frames--by using functions from `dplyr`; we can also combine our own functions with `dplyr`.

For example, when we use a `filter` function, we are asking R to check the value in a column in the first row, then determine whether that condition is met (and, therefore, whether to retain the row), then to do the same thing for the next row and the next...

Again, an important exception is when we use `if`-`else` statements inside our functions. To use those functions in `mutate()`, we need to use the `rowwise()` function.

```{r}
temps_df <- as.data.frame(temps)

# doesn't work; functions with if-else statements are NOT vectorized
# temps_df |>
#   dplyr::mutate(category = hot_or_cold(temps))

# this works!
temps_df |>
  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(category = hot_or_cold(temps))
```

1	---
2	title: "Week 13: Iteration"
3	author: "Ellen Bledsoe"
4	format: pdf
5	editor: visual
6	---
7	
8	```{r setup, include=FALSE}
9	knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
10	```
11	
12	# Iteration
13	
14	In this week's lesson, we will be talking about how to do repetitive tasks.
15	
16	As it turns out, computers are really good at repeating tasks. We call this repetition of the same task "iteration."
17	
18	There are many ways to iterate in R (we will look at a few others at the end of the lesson), but this week focuses on loops, which give us complete control over any kind of repetition we want.
19	
20	Specifically, we will use `for` loops, which perform the same action for each item in a list of things.
21	
22	## The `for` Loop
23	
24	Loops are the fundamental structure for repetition in programming.
25	
26	In particular, `for` loops perform the same action for each item in a list of things.
27	
28	The general structure of a `for` loop is below:
29	
30	```{r}
31	# for (item in list_of_items) {
32	#   do_something(item)
33	# }
34	```
35	
36	To see an example of this, let's calculate biomasses from volumes using a loop. If we want to see the results of the loop, we need to print them out.
37	
38	In this loop, we are going to use a `print()` function to display our results for each mass.
39	
40	```{r}
41	# vector of volumes
42	volumes <- c(1.6, 3, 8)
43	
44	# for each volume value in a vector of volumes
45	for (vol in volumes){           # perform some task inside the {}
46	  biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9   # calculate a mass
47	  print(biomass)                # print out the mass
48	}
49	```
50	
51	The code that is inside of the curly brackets will run once for each value in `volumes`. The `vol` object is a placeholder, representing one value from `volumes` at a time.
52	
53	The loop takes the first value from `volumes` and assigns it to the object `vol`. It performs the code inside the curly brackets, calculating the biomass and then printing the result.
54	
55	Once the code hits the end of what is enclosed inside the curly brackets, it starts the code all over again from the beginning using the next item in the list (or the `volumes` vector, in this case). The code takes the second value from `volumes`, assigns it to `vol`, does the calculation and prints the output.
56	
57	It continues to repeat this process--running the code with one value, then starting the whole process over again with the next value--until it has run through every element in the list.
58	
59	Ultimately, the loop above is doing the exact same thing as the code below, but in a more condensed and more flexible way.
60	
61	```{r}
62	# same as the for loop above
63	vol <- volumes[1]
64	biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
65	print(biomass)
66	
67	vol <- volumes[2]
68	biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
69	print(biomass)
70	
71	vol <- volumes[3]
72	biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
73	print(biomass)
74	```
75	
76	### Let's Practice!
77	
78	| Work on Questions 1a and 1b in the Assignment.
79	
80	## Looping with an Index
81	
82	Loops are iterating over a series of elements in a vector or other list-like object. When we use that value directly, this is called looping by value.
83	
84	There is another way to loop: *looping by index*
85	
86	- We often use `i` (for "index") as the placeholder.
87	- We use `1:length(volumes)` so the loop works no matter how many values there are. (For a data frame, we use `nrow()`.)
88	
89	```{r}
90	volumes <- c(1.6, 3, 8)
91	
92	for (i in 1:length(volumes)){          # i will be 1, then 2, then 3
93	   biomass <- 2.65 * volumes[i] ^ 0.9  # volumes[i] is the ith volume
94	   print(biomass)
95	}
96	```
97	
98	This new version of the loop gives us the same result as our original loop, but it's more complicated to understand. So why would we want to loop by index?
99	
100	The most common reason is to store the results in the same order (position) as the values we used to calculate them.
101	
102	### Storing Results
103	
104	To store results, we create an empty object *before* the loop starts. The `vector` function makes an empty vector:
105	
106	- `mode` is the type of data we are going to store
107	- `length` is the number of items in the vector
108	
109	```{r}
110	biomasses <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = length(volumes))
111	biomasses
112	```
113	
114	For each trip through the loop, we put the output into the `i`th position in the empty vector.
115	
116	```{r}
117	for (i in 1:length(volumes)){
118	   biomass <- 2.65 * volumes[i] ^ 0.9
119	   biomasses[i] <- biomass
120	}
121	
122	biomasses
123	```
124	
125	So far, we've talked about looping through one group of values (in a vector).
126	
127	Looping with an index also allows us to access values from multiple vectors.
128	
129	```{r}
130	# vectors
131	a_values <- c(2.65, 1.28, 3.29)
132	b_values <- c(0.9, 1.1, 1.2)
133	volumes <- c(1.6, 3, 8)
134	
135	# empty vector for results
136	biomasses <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = length(volumes))
137	
138	# for loop
139	for (i in 1:length(volumes)){
140	   biomass <- a_values[i] * volumes[i] ^ b_values[i]
141	   biomasses[i] <- biomass
142	}
143	
144	biomasses
145	```
146	
147	### Let's Practice!
148	
149	| Work on Questions 1c, 1d, and 1e in the Assignment.
150	
151	## Looping over Data Frames
152	
153	Several vectors of the same length, lined up by position...that is exactly what the columns of a data frame are!
154	
155	Most of the time, the values we want to loop over will be in a data frame.
156	
157	```{r}
158	# create an data frame
159	data <- data.frame(a = a_values, # column_name = values to fill
160	                   b = b_values, 
161	                   volume = volumes)
162	data
163	```
164	
165	To loop over rows, we loop by index from 1 to `nrow()`, and use `$` with `[i]` to grab the value in a specific column for the i-th row.
166	
167	To store the resulting values, we can create a new, empty column first.
168	
169	This is also where loops really shine: we can put an `if`-`else` statement directly inside a loop. Let's say we only want to calculate a biomass if the volume is less than 5.
170	
171	```{r}
172	# new, empty column
173	data$biomass <- NA
174	
175	for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
176	  # calculate biomass if biomass is less than 5
177	  if (data$volume[i] < 5) {
178	    biomass <- data$a[i] * data$volume[i] ^ data$b[i]
179	  } else {
180	    biomass <- NA
181	  }
182	  data$biomass[i] <- biomass
183	}
184	
185	data
186	```
187	
188	Realistically, I find myself putting `if`-`else` statements inside `for` loops, like the structure above, rather frequently.
189	
190	### Looping with Functions
191	
192	We can also call functions inside of loops.
193	
194	Remember that functions containing `if`-`else` statements are not vectorized, so we can't just give them a whole column; a loop solves that.
195	
196	```{r}
197	# write est_biomass function
198	est_biomass <- function(volume, a, b){
199	  # estimate biomass when volume is less than 5
200	  if (volume < 5) {
201	    biomass <- a * volume ^ b
202	  } else {
203	    biomass <- NA
204	  }
205	  return(biomass)
206	}
207	```
208	
209	We can't pass the vector to the function and get back a vector of results because `if`-`else` statements are not vectorized.
210	
211	```{r}
212	#| eval: false
213	est_biomass(volume = data$volume,
214	            a = data$a,
215	            b = data$b)
216	```
217	
218	Instead, we can loop over the values.
219	
220	```{r}
221	# loop through values in est_biomass
222	for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
223	  # save output into correct position in new column
224	  data$biomass[i] <- est_biomass(data$volume[i], data$a[i], data$b[i])
225	}
226	
227	data
228	```
229	
230	::: callout-note
231	## Do you need a loop?
232	
233	For a calculation within a single data frame, using `mutate()` is usually simpler.
234	
235	Most functions in the `tidyverse`, like `if_else()`, are vectorized so they work inside `mutate()` without a loop:
236	
237	```{r}
238	data |>
239	  dplyr::mutate(biomass = dplyr::if_else(volume < 5, 
240	                                         true = a * volume ^ b, 
241	                                         false = NA))
242	```
243	
244	Loops are most useful when the repetition involves several steps or goes beyond one data frame, like working through many files (coming up below!).
245	:::
246	
247	### Let's Practice!
248	
249	| Work on Question 2 in the Assignment.
250	
251	## Troubleshooting Loops
252	
253	Occasionally (okay, maybe often...) when you write a for loop, it will either give you an error or it will runn successfully run but give results you didn't anticipated.
254	
255	Since loops (like functions) have some kind of placeholder in them (such as `i` for index), the best way to figure out what is going on is to set the placeholder equal to a specific value and run each line of code between the `{}` to check every step individually.
256	
257	```{r}
258	#| eval: false
259	
260	data$biomass <- NA
261	
262	for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
263	  if (data$volume[i] < 5) {
264	    data$biomass[i] <- data$a[i] * data$volume[i] ^ data$b[i]
265	  } else {
266	    data$biomass <- NA
267	  }
268	}
269	
270	data
271	
272	# in the console, set i = to a number; run the entire code chunk line by line
273	# i = 2
274	# i = 3
275	```
276	
277	If part of your loop is working but another part isn't, find a value (or row) that should trigger the part that isn't working and set the index to that value.
278	
279	## Looping over Files
280	
281	While we often want to repeat things within our data, either in vectors or data frames, there are other instances when we might want to repeat the same task.
282	
283	For example, if we have many similar files, we might want to repeat the same tasks for all of those files.
284	
285	To demonstrate, let's download some simulated satellite collar data. Make sure you change the file paths accordingly to match the sub-directories in your RStudio Project, as needed.
286	
287	```{r}
288	download.file(url = "http://www.datacarpentry.org/semester-biology/data/locations.zip",
289	              destfile = "../data_raw/locations.zip") # where to put the zip file
290	
291	# unzip() function to open the zip file
292	# zipfile argument is the location of the file to be unzipped
293	# exdir argument is the location where the "extracted" files should be placed
294	unzip(zipfile = "../data_raw/locations.zip", exdir = "../data_raw/")
295	```
296	
297	Before we can loop through these files, we need to get the names of all of these files. The `list.files()` function will, well, list the files in the directory.
298	
299	We want only the data files we downloaded, so we'll add the optional `pattern` argument to only get the text files (end with `.txt`).
300	
301	The pattern argument can also take regular expressions if you need to be more nuanced about which files to include.
302	
303	```{r}
304	# in regex, .* means any character (.) any number of times (*)
305	# "locations.*.txt" indicates any file starting with "locations" and ending with ".txt"
306	data_files <- list.files(path = "../data_raw/", 
307	                         pattern = "locations.*.txt")
308	data_files
309	```
310	
311	### Storing Loop Results in a Data Frame
312	
313	Let's say we want to know the file name, count the number of observations, and get the minimum latitude value for each file. Since we are collecting several pieces of infor
314	
315	We would start by creating an empty data frame with `data.frame()`. Each argument is for one column: `column_name = an empty vector of the correct type and length`
316	
317	```{r}
318	num_files <- length(data_files)
319	
320	results <- data.frame(file_name = vector("character", num_files), # mode, length
321	                      count = vector("integer", num_files),
322	                      min_lat = vector("numeric", num_files))
323	results
324	```
325	
326	Then we loop over the files, read each one in, and store the information in the `i`th row of the appropriate column (e.g., `results$count[i]`).
327	
328	```{r}
329	for (i in 1:num_files){
330	
331	  # read in the data file
332	  filename <- data_files[i]
333	  locations <- read.csv(paste0("../data_raw/", filename))
334	
335	  # add information about the data file into the data frame
336	  results$file_name[i] <- filename
337	  results$count[i] <- nrow(locations)
338	  results$min_lat[i] <- min(locations$lat)
339	
340	}
341	
342	results
343	```
344	
345	### Let's Practice!
346	
347	| Work on Question 3 in the Assignment.
348	
349	## Other Ways to Iterate in R
350	
351	While this lesson focused on `for` loops, there are actually many ways to iterate in R. I've included a quick overview below.
352	
353	#### 1. Using `apply` or `map` Functions
354	
355	Both of these are families of functions. They take a function and apply that function to each item in a list of items.
356	
357	The `apply` functions (e.g., `apply`, `lapply`, `sapply`) are base R; you can learn more about how to use them [here](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2022/03/complete-tutorial-on-using-apply-functions-in-r/).
358	
359	The `map` functions come from the `purrr` package, part of the `tidyverse`. [Chapter 26: Iteration](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/iteration) in the "R for Data Science (2e)" book is a good starting point, as is the [`purrr` cheatsheet](https://purrr.tidyverse.org/).
360	
361	```{r}
362	hot_or_cold <- function(temp){
363	  if (temp > 72) {
364	    category <- "hot"
365	  } else {
366	    category <- "cold"
367	  }
368	  return(category)
369	}
370	
371	temps <- c(47.2, 72, 100)
372	
373	# base R
374	sapply(temps, hot_or_cold)
375	
376	# purrr from tidyverse
377	purrr::map(temps, hot_or_cold)
378	```
379	
380	#### 2. In data frames, using `dplyr` (mostly)
381	
382	We've actually already been iterating quite a bit--specifically in data frames--by using functions from `dplyr`; we can also combine our own functions with `dplyr`.
383	
384	For example, when we use a `filter` function, we are asking R to check the value in a column in the first row, then determine whether that condition is met (and, therefore, whether to retain the row), then to do the same thing for the next row and the next...
385	
386	Again, an important exception is when we use `if`-`else` statements inside our functions. To use those functions in `mutate()`, we need to use the `rowwise()` function.
387	
388	```{r}
389	temps_df <- as.data.frame(temps)
390	
391	# doesn't work; functions with if-else statements are NOT vectorized
392	# temps_df |>
393	#   dplyr::mutate(category = hot_or_cold(temps))
394	
395	# this works!
396	temps_df |>
397	  dplyr::rowwise() |>
398	  dplyr::mutate(category = hot_or_cold(temps))
399	```
400	
401	### Let's Practice!
402	
403	You should now have all the skills you need to complete the assignment, including the optional parts of Question 4!

```

# Iteration

In this week's lesson, we will be talking about how to do repetitive tasks.

As it turns out, computers are really good at repeating tasks. We call this repetition of the same task "iteration."

There are many ways to iterate in R (we will look at a few others at the end of the lesson), but this week focuses on loops, which give us complete control over any kind of repetition we want.

Specifically, we will use `for` loops, which perform the same action for each item in a list of things.

## The `for` Loop

Loops are the fundamental structure for repetition in programming.

In particular, `for` loops perform the same action for each item in a list of things.

The general structure of a `for` loop is below:

```{r}
# for (item in list_of_items) {
#   do_something(item)
# }
```

To see an example of this, let's calculate biomasses from volumes using a loop. If we want to see the results of the loop, we need to print them out.

In this loop, we are going to use a `print()` function to display our results for each mass.

```{r}
# vector of volumes
volumes <- c(1.6, 3, 8)

# for each volume value in a vector of volumes
for (vol in volumes){           # perform some task inside the {}
  biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9   # calculate a mass
  print(biomass)                # print out the mass
}
```

The code that is inside of the curly brackets will run once for each value in `volumes`. The `vol` object is a placeholder, representing one value from `volumes` at a time.

The loop takes the first value from `volumes` and assigns it to the object `vol`. It performs the code inside the curly brackets, calculating the biomass and then printing the result.

Once the code hits the end of what is enclosed inside the curly brackets, it starts the code all over again from the beginning using the next item in the list (or the `volumes` vector, in this case). The code takes the second value from `volumes`, assigns it to `vol`, does the calculation and prints the output.

It continues to repeat this process--running the code with one value, then starting the whole process over again with the next value--until it has run through every element in the list.

Ultimately, the loop above is doing the exact same thing as the code below, but in a more condensed and more flexible way.

```{r}
# same as the for loop above
vol <- volumes[1]
biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
print(biomass)

vol <- volumes[2]
biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
print(biomass)

vol <- volumes[3]
biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
print(biomass)
```

### Let's Practice!

| Work on Questions 1a and 1b in the Assignment.

## Looping with an Index

Loops are iterating over a series of elements in a vector or other list-like object. When we use that value directly, this is called looping by value.

There is another way to loop: *looping by index*

- We often use `i` (for "index") as the placeholder.
- We use `1:length(volumes)` so the loop works no matter how many values there are. (For a data frame, we use `nrow()`.)

```{r}
volumes <- c(1.6, 3, 8)

for (i in 1:length(volumes)){          # i will be 1, then 2, then 3
   biomass <- 2.65 * volumes[i] ^ 0.9  # volumes[i] is the ith volume
   print(biomass)
}
```

This new version of the loop gives us the same result as our original loop, but it's more complicated to understand. So why would we want to loop by index?

The most common reason is to store the results in the same order (position) as the values we used to calculate them.

### Storing Results

To store results, we create an empty object *before* the loop starts. The `vector` function makes an empty vector:

- `mode` is the type of data we are going to store
- `length` is the number of items in the vector

```{r}
biomasses <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = length(volumes))
biomasses
```

For each trip through the loop, we put the output into the `i`th position in the empty vector.

```{r}
for (i in 1:length(volumes)){
   biomass <- 2.65 * volumes[i] ^ 0.9
   biomasses[i] <- biomass
}

biomasses
```

So far, we've talked about looping through one group of values (in a vector).

Looping with an index also allows us to access values from multiple vectors.

```{r}
# vectors
a_values <- c(2.65, 1.28, 3.29)
b_values <- c(0.9, 1.1, 1.2)
volumes <- c(1.6, 3, 8)

# empty vector for results
biomasses <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = length(volumes))

# for loop
for (i in 1:length(volumes)){
   biomass <- a_values[i] * volumes[i] ^ b_values[i]
   biomasses[i] <- biomass
}

biomasses
```

### Let's Practice!

| Work on Questions 1c, 1d, and 1e in the Assignment.

## Looping over Data Frames

Several vectors of the same length, lined up by position...that is exactly what the columns of a data frame are!

Most of the time, the values we want to loop over will be in a data frame.

```{r}
# create an data frame
data <- data.frame(a = a_values, # column_name = values to fill
                   b = b_values, 
                   volume = volumes)
data
```

To loop over rows, we loop by index from 1 to `nrow()`, and use `$` with `[i]` to grab the value in a specific column for the i-th row.

To store the resulting values, we can create a new, empty column first.

This is also where loops really shine: we can put an `if`-`else` statement directly inside a loop. Let's say we only want to calculate a biomass if the volume is less than 5.

```{r}
# new, empty column
data$biomass <- NA

for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
  # calculate biomass if biomass is less than 5
  if (data$volume[i] < 5) {
    biomass <- data$a[i] * data$volume[i] ^ data$b[i]
  } else {
    biomass <- NA
  }
  data$biomass[i] <- biomass
}

data
```

Realistically, I find myself putting `if`-`else` statements inside `for` loops, like the structure above, rather frequently.

### Looping with Functions

We can also call functions inside of loops.

Remember that functions containing `if`-`else` statements are not vectorized, so we can't just give them a whole column; a loop solves that.

```{r}
# write est_biomass function
est_biomass <- function(volume, a, b){
  # estimate biomass when volume is less than 5
  if (volume < 5) {
    biomass <- a * volume ^ b
  } else {
    biomass <- NA
  }
  return(biomass)
}
```

We can't pass the vector to the function and get back a vector of results because `if`-`else` statements are not vectorized.

```{r}
#| eval: false
est_biomass(volume = data$volume,
            a = data$a,
            b = data$b)
```

Instead, we can loop over the values.

```{r}
# loop through values in est_biomass
for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
  # save output into correct position in new column
  data$biomass[i] <- est_biomass(data$volume[i], data$a[i], data$b[i])
}

data
```

::: callout-note
## Do you need a loop?

For a calculation within a single data frame, using `mutate()` is usually simpler.

Most functions in the `tidyverse`, like `if_else()`, are vectorized so they work inside `mutate()` without a loop:

```{r}
data |>
  dplyr::mutate(biomass = dplyr::if_else(volume < 5, 
                                         true = a * volume ^ b, 
                                         false = NA))
```

Loops are most useful when the repetition involves several steps or goes beyond one data frame, like working through many files (coming up below!).
:::

### Let's Practice!

| Work on Question 2 in the Assignment.

## Troubleshooting Loops

Occasionally (okay, maybe often...) when you write a for loop, it will either give you an error or it will runn successfully run but give results you didn't anticipated.

Since loops (like functions) have some kind of placeholder in them (such as `i` for index), the best way to figure out what is going on is to set the placeholder equal to a specific value and run each line of code between the `{}` to check every step individually.

```{r}
#| eval: false

data$biomass <- NA

for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
  if (data$volume[i] < 5) {
    data$biomass[i] <- data$a[i] * data$volume[i] ^ data$b[i]
  } else {
    data$biomass <- NA
  }
}

data

# in the console, set i = to a number; run the entire code chunk line by line
# i = 2
# i = 3
```

If part of your loop is working but another part isn't, find a value (or row) that should trigger the part that isn't working and set the index to that value.

## Looping over Files

While we often want to repeat things within our data, either in vectors or data frames, there are other instances when we might want to repeat the same task.

For example, if we have many similar files, we might want to repeat the same tasks for all of those files.

To demonstrate, let's download some simulated satellite collar data. Make sure you change the file paths accordingly to match the sub-directories in your RStudio Project, as needed.

```{r}
download.file(url = "http://www.datacarpentry.org/semester-biology/data/locations.zip",
              destfile = "../data_raw/locations.zip") # where to put the zip file

# unzip() function to open the zip file
# zipfile argument is the location of the file to be unzipped
# exdir argument is the location where the "extracted" files should be placed
unzip(zipfile = "../data_raw/locations.zip", exdir = "../data_raw/")
```

Before we can loop through these files, we need to get the names of all of these files. The `list.files()` function will, well, list the files in the directory.

We want only the data files we downloaded, so we'll add the optional `pattern` argument to only get the text files (end with `.txt`).

The pattern argument can also take regular expressions if you need to be more nuanced about which files to include.

```{r}
# in regex, .* means any character (.) any number of times (*)
# "locations.*.txt" indicates any file starting with "locations" and ending with ".txt"
data_files <- list.files(path = "../data_raw/", 
                         pattern = "locations.*.txt")
data_files
```

### Storing Loop Results in a Data Frame

Let's say we want to know the file name, count the number of observations, and get the minimum latitude value for each file. Since we are collecting several pieces of infor

We would start by creating an empty data frame with `data.frame()`. Each argument is for one column: `column_name = an empty vector of the correct type and length`

```{r}
num_files <- length(data_files)

results <- data.frame(file_name = vector("character", num_files), # mode, length
                      count = vector("integer", num_files),
                      min_lat = vector("numeric", num_files))
results
```

Then we loop over the files, read each one in, and store the information in the `i`th row of the appropriate column (e.g., `results$count[i]`).

```{r}
for (i in 1:num_files){

  # read in the data file
  filename <- data_files[i]
  locations <- read.csv(paste0("../data_raw/", filename))

  # add information about the data file into the data frame
  results$file_name[i] <- filename
  results$count[i] <- nrow(locations)
  results$min_lat[i] <- min(locations$lat)

}

results
```

### Let's Practice!

| Work on Question 3 in the Assignment.

## Other Ways to Iterate in R

While this lesson focused on `for` loops, there are actually many ways to iterate in R. I've included a quick overview below.

#### 1. Using `apply` or `map` Functions

Both of these are families of functions. They take a function and apply that function to each item in a list of items.

The `apply` functions (e.g., `apply`, `lapply`, `sapply`) are base R; you can learn more about how to use them [here](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2022/03/complete-tutorial-on-using-apply-functions-in-r/).

The `map` functions come from the `purrr` package, part of the `tidyverse`. [Chapter 26: Iteration](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/iteration) in the "R for Data Science (2e)" book is a good starting point, as is the [`purrr` cheatsheet](https://purrr.tidyverse.org/).

```{r}
hot_or_cold <- function(temp){
  if (temp > 72) {
    category <- "hot"
  } else {
    category <- "cold"
  }
  return(category)
}

temps <- c(47.2, 72, 100)

# base R
sapply(temps, hot_or_cold)

# purrr from tidyverse
purrr::map(temps, hot_or_cold)
```

#### 2. In data frames, using `dplyr` (mostly)

We've actually already been iterating quite a bit--specifically in data frames--by using functions from `dplyr`; we can also combine our own functions with `dplyr`.

For example, when we use a `filter` function, we are asking R to check the value in a column in the first row, then determine whether that condition is met (and, therefore, whether to retain the row), then to do the same thing for the next row and the next...

Again, an important exception is when we use `if`-`else` statements inside our functions. To use those functions in `mutate()`, we need to use the `rowwise()` function.

```{r}
temps_df <- as.data.frame(temps)

# doesn't work; functions with if-else statements are NOT vectorized
# temps_df |>
#   dplyr::mutate(category = hot_or_cold(temps))

# this works!
temps_df |>
  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(category = hot_or_cold(temps))
```

### Let's Practice!

You should now have all the skills you need to complete the assignment, including the optional parts of Question 4!
